#725. Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy

More than 100 years after Albert Einstein developed his theory of gravity, physicists have uncovered a surprising possibility hidden within his equations. Their work suggests that gravitational fields can undergo a process in which their underlying structures break and reconnect, allowing energy to flow from gravity into matter.

The phenomenon, known as "gravitational reconnection," bears an unexpected resemblance to a process responsible for some of the Sun's most powerful eruptions. Researchers believe this connection could provide new insights into how gravity behaves under extreme conditions, including during collisions between black holes.

The discovery comes from Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's Departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile. By examining Einstein's equations from a different mathematical perspective, they identified a remarkable similarity between gravity and the behavior of electrically charged gases known as plasmas.

Their approach could help scientists uncover fundamental rules governing the behavior of gravitational fields. Such insights are especially valuable in regions where gravity severely distorts space-time, making even the most powerful computer simulations difficult to interpret.

How Gravity Could Behave Like a Solar Flare

The key to understanding this discovery lies in a well-known phenomenon called magnetic reconnection. Magnetic fields are often illustrated using curved lines, such as the patterns formed by iron filings around a magnet or the enormous magnetic loops extending above the Sun's surface.

In a plasma, which consists of electrically charged particles, these magnetic field lines can be pulled, twisted, and stretched. Under certain conditions, they undergo a sudden change in their connections, releasing stored magnetic energy into the surrounding particles. This process powers solar flares and ranks among the most important mechanisms for releasing energy throughout the universe.

"Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration," Comisso said. "When they break and reconnect, they release energy."

The resulting energy transfer can produce extraordinarily powerful events. As Comisso explained, "It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events."

The researchers found that gravitational fields may undergo an analogous transformation. However, gravity operates within Einstein's four-dimensional space-time, which includes three dimensions of space and one dimension of time. This makes its underlying mathematical structure different from that of an ordinary magnetic field.

Gravitational Reconnection and the Fabric of Space-Time

"Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field 'sheets' rather than field lines," explained Comisso. "Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a 'sheet.'"

In this mathematical description, gravity is represented by sheets rather than individual field lines. Just as magnetic field lines can change their connections and release energy, these gravitational sheets can also rearrange their connections under the appropriate conditions.

Importantly, the sheets are mathematical representations, not physical surfaces that literally tear apart. Their reconnection describes a way for the gravitational field to transfer energy into matter.

The researchers arrived at this result by exploring properties of Einstein's equations that are not obvious in their usual mathematical form. Their work builds on an earlier investigation that revealed previously unrecognized restrictions on how space-time can bend, stretch, and change over time.

The new study, titled "Reconnection of Gravitational Fields," was published in Physical Review D, a journal of the American Physical Society. It extends findings from an earlier study published in Physical Review Letters by Comisso, Asenjo, and Maricarmen A. Winkler.

That earlier work identified mathematical constraints that determine which changes in the geometry of space-time are possible. Although these restrictions are built into Einstein's theory, they had not previously been recognized in this form.

"Einstein's equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent," said Asenjo. "By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves."

In their latest research, Comisso and Asenjo investigated what happens when the ideal conditions that normally preserve connections within gravitational field structures no longer hold. They found that those connections can change, producing the phenomenon they call gravitational reconnection.

"Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them," Comisso said. "You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior."

Why Plasma Physics Offers New Clues About Gravity

The breakthrough depends on a different mathematical formulation of Einstein's equations developed by physicists in recent years. Although this formulation uses different variables, it is mathematically equivalent to the original equations and describes the same underlying physics.

What makes it particularly useful is its resemblance to equations used to study plasmas. These electrically charged gases make up the Sun, are used in nuclear fusion experiments, and occupy much of the space between stars.

Comisso has devoted his career to understanding plasma behavior. When he and his colleagues recognized the mathematical similarities between plasma physics and gravity, they realized that methods developed to study magnetic fields could also reveal previously overlooked properties of gravitational fields.

This approach allows physicists to identify patterns and restrictions governing space-time without necessarily solving every part of Einstein's equations.

"It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time," Comisso said. "Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints."

Rather than relying entirely on complex numerical calculations, researchers can use these underlying rules to determine which behaviors are physically possible. This could provide a valuable new perspective on gravitational events that are exceptionally difficult to model.

What Gravitational Reconnection Could Mean for Black Holes

One of the most promising applications involves black hole collisions. When two black holes approach and merge, their immense gravitational fields produce extreme distortions in space-time.

To understand these events, astrophysicists typically rely on massive supercomputer simulations. Researchers specify the initial conditions, calculate how the system changes over time, and examine the resulting behavior.

These simulations help scientists predict the gravitational waves generated by merging black holes. Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time that can be detected by instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which is designed to measure the extraordinarily small distortions produced by powerful cosmic events.

The newly identified rules governing gravitational fields could complement these simulations by revealing patterns that might otherwise be difficult to recognize. They may also help researchers better understand how energy is transferred during some of the universe's most extreme gravitational interactions.

For now, gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical finding. Scientists have not yet established how the process operates in actual astrophysical environments or whether its effects can be observed.

The next step is to investigate gravitational reconnection in specific situations, particularly when black holes merge. Comisso hopes this research will eventually make it possible to estimate how much energy such events release and determine whether gravitational reconnection produces recognizable signatures in gravitational wave signals.

If those predictions can be developed and tested, the approach could offer a powerful new way to investigate the behavior of gravity under extreme conditions, revealing more of the physics concealed within Einstein's century-old equations.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation and NASA.

Materials provided by Columbia University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"The door was open on this theory — that Little Red Dots could be primordial black holes. We've now cracked it open a little farther."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ever since NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) started observing the early universe, it has been providing almost as many surprises as it has answers. One such surprise are the so-called Little Red Dots, cosmic objects that seemingly disappear completely before the universe is two billion years old.

New research suggests that Little Red Dots may actually be connected primordial black holes, tiny black holes born not from dying stars but rather from fluctuations in the density of matter just after the Big Bang, in the earliest moments of cosmic history. Should they exist, primordial black holes would predate stars, galactic dust particles, and elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Now, researchers have used JWST data to test whether one particular Little Red Dot, known as blackAbell 2744-QSO1 (QSO1), could host a primordial black hole.

"A black hole is an object born from the gravitational death of a star. Primordial black holes are a very different story," study team member Valerio De Luca, of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Johns Hopkins University (JHU) in Maryland, said in a statement.

"They come from the physics of the early universe that predates the first stars, when the universe was expanding exponentially in time and space. So the mechanisms for creating primordial black holes are different," De Luca added.

Though scientists have theorized about the existence of primordial black holes since they were first proposed by Stephen Hawking in the 1970s, no hard evidence has presented itself. One of the issues scientists have puzzled over is how to tell the difference between a primordial black hole and a "traditional" or astrophysical black hole formed from the supernova death and collapse of a massive star.

"Little Red Dots could surround astrophysical black holes, and most probably many of them do, but they could also be primordial black holes, if primordial black holes exist," De Luca said. "So the question becomes, Which ones are primordial and how can we tell?"

De Luca and colleagues turned their attention to QS01, located around 13.1 billion light-years from Earth, which is seen as it was just 700 million years after the Big Bang. What makes this Little Red Dot stand out is the fact that it is almost entirely composed of hydrogen and helium. Because these were the universe's first elements, it could be more unspoiled and primordial than other Little Red Dots.

The team modeled how a Little Red Dot like QS01 could form from a primordial black hole. That was necessary because the circumstances under which this could happen would have to be very specific.

"There are constraints on primordial black holes from cosmological observations," said team member Loris Del Grosso, also of JHU's Department of Physics and Astronomy. "There can only be so many primordial black holes in the universe, for example, and there cannot be too many of them in a given cluster."

Considering three possible scenarios, the team found that the most likely situation is a smaller primordial black hole consuming surrounding gas and energy until it grew to be the size of QSO1.

"The door was open on this theory — that Little Red Dots could be primordial black holes," Del Grosso said. "We've now cracked it open a little farther by showing some scenarios are more likely than others."

Del Grosso and crew now intend to look at the other 100 or so Little Red Dots seen by the JWST to determine how many of them could have started life as primordial black holes.

Then scientists may finally have the evidence to say these long-theorized ancient black holes actually existed.

"We don't have a clear understanding of what happens in the early universe right after the Big Bang," De Luca concluded. "If primordial black holes do exist, then something had to happen to make them in the first place, which would be a groundbreaking discovery in physics."

The team's findings were published in June in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #721. A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer

For some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends. Memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and persistent exhaustion can interfere with everyday life, sometimes for years. Now, researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have found promising early evidence that a supplement containing a naturally occurring molecule could help relieve these symptoms.

The molecule, called oxaloacetate, is already present in the human body and plays an important role in how cells generate energy. In a small clinical trial, breast cancer survivors who took the supplement for eight weeks reported noticeable improvements in thinking, memory, concentration, and fatigue.

The results, published in JCO Oncology Advances, also showed improvements on cognitive tests measuring how quickly participants processed information and performed tasks requiring planning, attention, and mental flexibility. Although larger studies are needed to confirm the findings, the results suggest a potentially new way to address a problem that has long been difficult to treat.

"Cancer-related cognitive impairment can persist long after treatment ends and can have a significant impact on a person's daily life, yet we still have very few effective treatments for it," said Dr. Patricia Ganz, the study's first author and a distinguished professor of medicine at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Why Brain Fog Can Persist After Cancer Treatment

Cognitive difficulties are a lasting concern for many people who survive breast cancer. Researchers estimate that roughly 15% to 25% experience ongoing problems with memory, concentration, or other thinking abilities after their diagnosis and treatment. These symptoms are often described as "chemo brain" or "brain fog."

Despite the name, chemotherapy is not necessarily the only cause. Scientists increasingly recognize that cancer-related cognitive impairment can develop through several overlapping processes. The cancer itself, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, inflammation, hormonal changes, and other biological and behavioral influences may all contribute.

Because the causes are complicated and effective treatments remain limited, researchers are investigating ways to address the underlying changes that may disrupt normal brain function.

One area of interest involves the relationship between inflammation, brain chemistry, and energy production. Inflammation linked to cancer and its treatments may interfere with glutamate signaling, an important part of communication between nerve cells. It may also disturb the processes that allow brain cells to produce and use energy efficiently. Together, these disruptions could contribute to difficulties with thinking and persistent mental exhaustion.

Oxaloacetate attracted the UCLA team's attention because it participates in both cellular energy production and the regulation of glutamate. The researchers wanted to learn whether providing additional oxaloacetate through a supplement might reduce the cognitive symptoms and fatigue experienced by cancer survivors.

Testing Oxaloacetate for Brain Fog and Fatigue

To investigate, the researchers carried out a phase II clinical trial involving 18 women who had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer between one and five years earlier. All participants were experiencing substantial cognitive difficulties when they entered the study.

The women were approximately 50 years old on average. Most had undergone chemotherapy, and nearly 90% were still receiving endocrine therapy during the trial.

Each participant was instructed to take 500 milligrams of oxaloacetate twice a day for eight weeks. The researchers tracked changes in cognitive symptoms using questionnaires completed by the participants, along with standardized tests designed to evaluate memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function. Executive function includes the mental abilities needed to organize activities, maintain focus, make plans, and manage tasks.

The study also examined fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression, physical health, and mental well-being. Throughout the treatment period, the team monitored participants for possible side effects.

Brain Fog Scores Improved After Eight Weeks

Of the 18 women enrolled, 16 completed the full eight weeks of supplementation. Every participant who finished the treatment reported significant improvement in her cognitive symptoms.

The changes were particularly striking on the study's main measure of perceived cognitive impairment. Before treatment, the participants had an average score of 29.1. After eight weeks, that average had climbed to 55.5, placing the group in the range considered normal rather than impaired.

Signs of improvement were already apparent after four weeks, and the benefits reported by participants generally became more pronounced as treatment continued.

The results extended beyond memory and concentration. Participants reported significantly less fatigue, including the mental exhaustion that can make everyday activities difficult. They also described meaningful improvements in their ability to function physically.

Standardized cognitive testing provided additional encouraging evidence. Researchers observed improvements in processing speed and executive function, suggesting that some aspects of thinking performance may have improved alongside the participants' perceptions of their symptoms.

However, the scientists emphasized that these results remain preliminary because the trial included so few participants.

Promising Results, but More Research Is Needed

Oxaloacetate was generally well tolerated during the eight-week study. The most frequently reported side effects involved the digestive system, including indigestion, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea.

Two women stopped taking the supplement because of gastrointestinal symptoms. No serious adverse events were recorded.

Despite the encouraging improvements, the researchers cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about the supplement's effectiveness. The trial was small and did not include a placebo group or another comparison group. Without that comparison, it is not possible to determine whether oxaloacetate itself caused the improvements.

"These early findings give us a strong reason to continue studying oxaloacetate as a potential approach for managing cognitive problems after breast cancer treatment," Ganz said.

Larger Clinical Trial Will Test the Supplement's Benefits

To build on these initial findings, the UCLA team has been preparing a randomized, placebo-controlled phase II clinical trial involving breast cancer survivors with cancer-related cognitive impairment. The study was expected to begin enrolling participants in late 2026.

By comparing oxaloacetate with a placebo, the researchers hope to establish whether the supplement produces measurable benefits beyond those that might occur without active treatment.

The investigators are also conducting preclinical research in mice to better understand how oxaloacetate affects the body and brain. These experiments include a placebo-controlled study examining whether the molecule produces similar improvements (improved fatigue and physical function) in animals.

The research received partial financial support from the Breast Cancer Research Foundation and the National Cancer Institute.

In addition to Ganz, the study's authors were Kathleen Van Dyk, PhD, Catherine M. Crespi, PhD, Laura Petersen, MS, Mina Sedrak, MD, MS, and Julienne Bower, PhD, all affiliated with UCLA.

Materials provided by University of California - Los Angeles Health Sciences. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#720. ‘Apart’ Star Luca Pasqualino and Creator Stelana Kliris Unpack a Love Story Amid War and Apartheid

The film, starring Leem Lubany and inspired by the experiences of the writer-director's parents who emigrated from Cyprus to South Africa, opens Tallinn's Critics' Picks program.

South African Cypriot writer-director Stelana Kliris’ parents emigrated from Cyprus and moved to South Africa, leaving one divided country for another. What is that experience like, you wonder? Now, you can go on a cinematic journey to travel back in time and across the world to find out. Kliris (Find Me Falling, Committed) has used the experiences of her refugee parents as inspiration and “translated this into a film that challenges the idea of ‘us’ and ‘them.'”

Apart is the movie‘s fitting title, and it stars Leem Lubany (Omar, Rock the Kasbah), Luca Pasqualino (Rivals, The Musketeers) and Girley Jazama (Under the Hanging Tree, The White Line). And with war and refugees constantly in the headlines, the film explores issues and challenges that feel particularly timely and topical. Related Stories Movies 'Bugonia,' 'Lord of the Flies' Among 2026 FilmLight Colour Awards Winners Business ITV Unveils "Temporary" Content Cost Cuts as Q3 Ad Revenue Drops 8 Percent Amid "Weaker" Demand

Apart will get its world premiere at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia on Friday, Nov. 13, opening its Critics’ Picks section.

“In 1974, when Turkey invades Cyprus, young Eleni (Lubany) leaves her homeland through an arranged marriage and finds herself in Apartheid South Africa, swapping one divided country for another,” teases a synopsis for the film. “There, a new life with Nico (Pasqualino) slowly turns into love, until an unexpected friendship forces her to confront a secret from her past.”

Kliris wrote and directed Apart and produced it with Susan Simnett, Jamie Harvey and Ioanna Bolomyti. The cinematographer is Simon Sarketzis, with Emilios Avraam handling editing. Reinvent Yellow Sales is handling sales. Watch a trailer for Apart right here.

Pasqualino, who is now back on Disney+ in the second part of season 2 of the hit show Rivals, and Kliris talked to THR about Apart, how it was shot in Cyprus and captures a 1970s aesthetic, casting challenges, and how urgent the themes explored in the film feel.

Stelana, how much of Apart is based on your family’s history and experience?

STELANA KLIRIS My parents are both from Cyprus. My mom was a refugee from the war, and they actually met in South Africa. I was born and raised there. I experienced Apartheid as a child as I grew up during the ’80s in South Africa. So I grew up with all of these stories from both my parents and my own experiences. The film was an opportunity to bring all of that together.

How did Luca come aboard, especially given his busy TV schedule?

STELANA KLIRIS Luca was just an absolute gem to find. We worked with casting director Nancy Bishop, but it’s a difficult film, politically and historically, and a lot of local talent was a little fearful of taking on the subject matter. So we went outside the island [of Cyprus], and I’m so glad we did.

Luca, how did you get into your character, Nico, and his struggles?

LUCA PASQUALINO I don’t come from a Cypriot or South African background, but I do come from an immigrant Italian background. So I’ve been very much brought up around these stories. My grandparents immigrated to England from Italy after the war and then had to go through the struggles of not being from that nation. They sacrificed so much and had to forget everything that they’d ever known, leave it all behind to create a better life for themselves. That part of Nico is part of my family’s history.

And it wasn’t just the financial struggles they faced, but also not knowing the language, not knowing anything about the country. They literally had to start again. So that part of the story very much resonated with me.

Apart has characters who are not black-and-white but complicated. For example, with Nico, I loved some of the things he says or does and hated others…

STELANA KLIRIS Yes, they are very complex characters. They are very flawed and human. That was very important to me. They are not based on a specific person, but [inspired by] all these characters and people that I grew up with who were never perfect and sometimes had to do something that is maybe a little wrong to survive.

It’s a very human element, and what’s great about both Luca and Leem is that they really brought out this complexity. These characters are very three-dimensional, and they were able to really bring them to life in this way. With Luca, you get to see this really great range, because he can be very vulnerable, but his character can also be really hard, and [over time] we understand why.

LUCA PASQUALINO Nico is a very proud man. It would break his heart if he wasn’t giving his family the best that he could possibly give them. So, yes, there’s a moral ambiguity to it. The rules are there to maybe be bent or broken in certain ways, and he denies it a lot of the time. But there comes a moment where something shifts in him and he realizes he needs to take risks in life. And he decides that he’s going to go down a slightly alternative route. He does what he feels that he has to do. He has a wife, and he has to provide and care and take matters into his own hands.

Did you have an accent coach or so, Luca? How did you develop the way Nico sounds?

LUCA PASQUALINO We got there with a lot of time, a lot of repetition and a lot of frustration at times. It takes a lot of hard work when you don’t speak the language. It’s difficult to understand intonation and the flow of dialogue. Early on, our dialect coach would say a line to me, and I thought I said it exactly how she did. But she said no. To my ear, it sounded exactly the same, but to hers it didn’t. So, I hope it’s not awful. I’m happy I got to have that experience, and I hope people can understand everything that we’re trying to say.

STELANA KLIRIS They worked with a really great dialect coach called Léa Maléni, and Luca had to learn Greek. And they had to speak with an accent. We had multiple dialect coaches. Girley Jazama is actually Namibian, so she had to learn to speak Sesotho. We had Turkish Cypriot actors on set, some of whom didn’t speak any English. So at some point, we had about three or four different dialect coaches and interpreters on set. And in between takes, trying to give notes and talking about the scene just became this cacophony of languages. It was a great multinational experience.

Was there any scene that was particularly difficult to shoot?

LUCA PASQUALINO Every day was a new challenge. I loved it. But the one thing that stands out the most was just trying to make one scene feel as tragic as possible. There’s a moment where Nico talks about his brother and how he was kidnapped and murdered. At one point, I fell into this hole of overthinking it. But a couple of days before [we shot it], I decided I knew the lines, but I was not going to think about it anymore. And then the day we shot that scene, I was just open to allowing it to happen. There is a moment that was not scripted. I just had to feel that heartbreak within me instead of trying to act.

Stelana, can you tell me a bit about the visual aesthetic of the film and where you shot it? There are scenes that look a bit like an old home video…

STELANA KLIRIS We shot all of it in Cyprus. We were supposed to shoot in South Africa as well, but it didn’t work out in the end, for various reasons. Cyprus still has a lot of ’70s aesthetics in terms of buildings and neighborhoods, but we did have to hide a lot of things. And whatever we didn’t manage to hide had to be erased with VFX.

We also used an 8-millimeter camera for a lot of scenes to give it that lovely ’70s home video look. In fact, a party scene in an apartment is an exact replica of home videos I have from my parents, where immigrant Cypriots gathered in little apartments and squeezed together, having parties. We used some archive footage as well, just to really make it as authentic as possible and really show South Africa in the ’70s. We’ve mixed it up. Some of it is our own, some of it is archive. Hopefully, you can’t really tell. It’s just all there to immerse people in that era.

Apart is a historic snapshot, but it also feels quite timely. Or maybe it’s timeless? What do you think?

STELANA KLIRIS I think it’s very relevant. I think everyone can relate to being young and struggling and trying to find your way in the world, regardless of the era or whether there’s a backdrop of war. It’s a very human story and very intimate. And it really tries to boil down to a human level the many problems that we still have, the same problems that we’ve had throughout history.

LUCA PASQUALINO All you have to do is turn on the news, and you can see that it’s happening all over the world. The unfortunate, sad reality is that for a lot of people, there is always something to fight over. Even if you were to take the war element out of the script, there are still so many other things going on.

The relationship between Nico and Eleni is the real heart of the film. It’s two people who, for their own reasons, are trying to find a better life, trying to escape, and they end up finding solace in each other. The war is the backdrop for a really emotional, heart-wrenching love story.

Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's award-winning exposé on Israel's war in Gaza has grossed more than $14 million at the box office to date.

NAZA hit a new box office milestone, with more than 1.5 million theatrical admissions worldwide.

The award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor looks at the alleged policies the Israeli Defense Force (IDF) uses to target and kill civilians in Gaza.

As of Friday, Nov. 6, NAZA racked up more than 1.54 million theatrical admissions across 47 territories, making it one of the most-watched theatrical docs of 2026.

The film premiered in Venice where it won the Special Jury Prize for directors Abraham and Szor. It was attacked by the right-wing in Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for the identification and prosecution of the film’s whistle-blower interviewees, and Israel’s culture minister threatened to strip the NAZA directors of their citizenship. Michael Tuckman’s mTuckman Media intially started a self release of NAZA in the U.S. on Sept. 30 before Neon came on in late October to expand the film’s theatrical release.

The strongest performance has been in Italy, where NAZA bowed at number one on Sept. 29 via distributor I Wonder. The film has grossed more than $6 million to date, making it the third most-watched documentary in the territory, behind only Fahrenheit 9/11 and The March of the Penguins.

In France, where the film received a special 48-hours event release, to get around French windowing rules, NAZA sold more than 82,000 tickets, topping the box office over the two days.

Jupiter and Mars will appear incredibly close as they shine in the constellation Leo on Nov. 15.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Jupiter and Mars will shine side by side in a spectacular close approach in the heart of the constellation Leo on Nov. 15. Here's what you need to know.

Mars and Jupiter reach their closest apparent separation in Earth's sky at 9:04 p.m. EST on Nov. 15 (0204 GMT on Nov. 16), according to astronomy website In-The-Sky. The planets will be below the horizon for U.S. stargazers at the moment of their closest approach, but observers can catch the pair rising above the eastern horizon around midnight local time, just a few hours later.

Remember: You can discover the exact timings for the rising and setting of the planets above your local horizon using Time and Date's night sky tracker.

Jupiter will be the brightest of the pair, when it rises a little over 1 degree from the red light of Mars — roughly the width of your little finger held at arm's length against the night sky. The bright star Regulus will glow close at hand, forming the dot of the backward question mark formation of stars that represents the head of the great Lion in the constellation Leo.

The Celestron StarSense Explorer LT114AZ is a great way to get a closer look at Jupiter, Mars and Saturn. Its 4.5-inch aperture and a high 1000mm focal length delivers good magnification out of the box, plus it's integrated with the StarSense smartphone app, which makes finding those planets so much easier. Check out our full review for more.

Mars and Jupiter will be close enough to share the field of view of a pair of 10x50 binoculars and will also make for a spectacular sight through the eyepiece of a telescope when viewed separately as they rise away from the horizon.

The gas giant's iconic Great Red Spot will rotate into view in the predawn hours of Nov. 16, and will be visible through a backyard telescope with an aperture of just 4 inches. Using a light green color filter will help increase the visibility of the vast storm, while an orange filter will help bring out detail in the gas giant's sweeping cloud belts.

The two planets will appear to gradually drift apart over the coming weeks and won't appear as close again for another 2.5 years in July 2029, when the two planets appear close together in the constellation Virgo.

Be sure to check out our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography if you're interested in following the dance of the planets for yourself.

#717. An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected new approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

The findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease."

Rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research showed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an important question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

Women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially important because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she said. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most."

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

#715. Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM

With Trump and bipartisan lawmakers on board, industry figures at AFM are hoping for action before Washington’s January power shift — and some financiers are already betting on passage.

Few issues loom larger over the projects being assembled at this week’s American Film Market, Los Angeles’ annual gathering of the independent movie industry, than the fate of a proposed U.S. federal production incentive.

“A federal incentive would change the entire nature of our film and TV industry,” Josh Rogin, the Motion Picture Association’s senior vp of federal government affairs, said Tuesday during an AFM panel.

But for all the optimism around the proposal, its backers are also growing a tad anxious. Producers want Congress to act before the year ends, while President Trump’s endorsement and a bipartisan coalition remain tenuously in place. Related Stories Movies 'Long Long Night' Director Youm Kyu-bock on Creating Animation That Takes Kids Seriously Movies Is the Hope at AFM Real?

“I believe very strongly that we’re going to get this accomplished, and we have to get this done before the end of the year so that we can start planning projects for 2027,” said Steven Paul, chairman and CEO of SP Media Group.

Paul and SP Media president Scott Karol have worked closely with actor Jon Voight, Trump’s “special ambassador” to Hollywood, to develop proposals to revive U.S. production and win the president’s backing. Their efforts, along with backing from the MPA, have helped turn the longstanding industry wish for a federal incentive into an exceedingly rare point of agreement between Trump, left-leaning Hollywood and lawmakers in both parties.

Trump publicly backed a federal incentive in August, and in September, senators Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act. House backers include Republicans Nathaniel Moran and Brian Jack alongside Democrats Linda Sánchez and Laura Friedman.

The proposal would provide a 20 percent credit on qualifying U.S. production wages, rising to a maximum of 30 percent with bonuses, including one for independent productions. It could supplement state incentives and would be transferable.

But the Democrats’ midterm “blue wave” has heightened the urgency for many. With the Senate targeting a Dec. 18 adjournment, advocates have roughly five weeks to secure the bill’s passage. Legislation left unfinished when the current lame-duck Congress ends would have to be reintroduced in the new Congress.

That could mean renewed debate over the credit’s cost and eligibility rules, alongside fresh bargaining over legislative priorities. And the bigger danger, say backers, is losing momentum as Washington’s attention shifts to the confrontation between Trump and incoming Democratic majorities. Many fear the president’s support could easily evaporate as both sides enter battle mode.

At an Oct. 30 campaign rally in Florida, Trump mocked Hollywood liberals for “kissing my ass” while seeking backing for the proposals.

“They want tax credits for Hollywood because Hollywood’s dying,” he told the crowd. “And I’ll probably do it. Should I do it? Probably.”

“It needs to get passed before the end of the year,” Karol said at AFM, “because who the hell knows what’s going to happen next year when the Democrats come in to take the House and the Senate, and then Trump gets upset because he’s a lame duck.”

Many also want swift passage so producers can plan their budgets and bank on the new support while industry momentum is running high at the box office, rather than face another bout of uncertainty.

“They need to know that if it gets passed in December, that any film that starts principal photography on or after Jan. 1 of 2027 will be able to qualify for this big new incentive — which will be amazing,” Karol added.

Some financiers at AFM have already begun positioning themselves for that possibility, and they’re allocating their investment dollars accordingly — in a way that is likely, despite the odds, to please both Trump and liberal Hollywood’s below-the-line workers. British producer-financier Head Gear Films has announced a U.S. operation and plans to invest $120 million in American independent film and television in its first year.

Its co-founder and CEO, Phil Hunt, sees a federal credit creating opportunities to finance U.S. productions using the same tax-credit lending model familiar in Britain and Europe.

“If it passes, a U.S. production gets cheaper to make,” Hunt said. “That’s why we’re setting up now, so we’re ready the day it lands.”

Scott Roxborough contributed to this report.

On Nov. 9, 1967, NASA launched the powerful new Saturn V rocket on its maiden voyage.

The Saturn V moon rocket was 363 feet tall. That's taller than the Statue of Liberty! It was the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built at the time (though SpaceX's Starship megarocket has since surpassed it). NASA needed such a powerful rocket to launch astronauts to the moon. However, the first Saturn V launch didn't carry astronauts, because it was only a test flight.

During the launch, the rocket created a loud shockwave that surprised nearby observers. The ground shook so hard that it rattled buildings miles away, and all the shaking caused a huge shower of dust and debris NASA's new launch center, the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The mission lasted 8 hours 36 minutes. The rocket carried an uncrewed command module that splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.

The launch of Apollo 4 in November 1967 was a turning point for NASA on its path to landing astronauts on the moon.

The space agency had bet the moon on its new Saturn V booster, a three-stage heavy-lift rocket designed to fly astronauts in a capsule (as well as their lander) to the moon and back. But the rocket had never been fully tested until the Apollo 4 launch.

NASA also needed a new launch site for its Apollo missions. So the agency built Launch Complex 39 at what is now called the Kennedy Space Center, a Florida spaceport that has become the home port for orbital human spaceflight in the United States. But in 1967, no rockets had ever flown from the site. Yet, everything went according to plan.

“It was really an expert launching all the way through from lifting off exactly on time to performance of every single stage,” rocket pioneer Wernher von Braun, director of NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, said at the time.

The launch came as NASA was on its heels.

Just months earlier, on Jan. 27, 1967, the space agency suffered a fatal tragedy when Apollo 1 astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee died on the launch pad after a fire broke out inside their Apollo command module during a ground test.

“The maiden voyage of the Saturn V dramatically increased the confidence of people across the nation in the management of the largest research and development undertaking in which the western world has ever engaged,” George Mueller, NASA's then-Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight, said at the time.

One year later, another Saturn V rocket launched the first astronauts to the moon with the Apollo 8 mission. All of the Apollo missions that followed also launched on Saturn V rockets.

Just two years after its debut, the Saturn V rocket launched the Apollo 11 astronauts to the moon for the first crewed moon landing in July 1969.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

#713. Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered

A tiny fish with brilliant orange markings has been discovered in the Brazilian Amazon, but scientists warn that the newly identified species may already be at risk of extinction. Found in a handful of forest pools threatened by human activity, the colorful fish has prompted researchers to call for urgent conservation measures.

The new species, named Laimosemion laranja, belongs to a group of small freshwater fish known as killifish. It measures less than three centimeters in standard length, but its appearance is anything but ordinary. Males have rows of bright orange spots along the front half of their bodies, followed by bold orange chevron patterns near the tail. These vivid markings stand out against their pale gray sides.

The discovery was made during fieldwork in the Rio Cajari drainage in southern Amapá, a state in northern Brazil. The research team included scientists from the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte, Instituto Peixe das Nuvens, Universidade Federal do Pará, and University of West Florida.

A Striking Discovery in the Amazon Rainforest

The researchers were exploring how different freshwater fish in the Rivulidae family have evolved their life cycles and survival strategies across Brazil's diverse environments. During their surveys, they encountered a fish whose unusual coloration immediately stood out.

"We are developing a research project aimed at investigating the evolution of life-history strategies in freshwater fishes of the family Rivulidae across different biomes in Brazil," said lead researcher Yuri Abrantes of the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte. "During our sampling in small rivers locally known as 'igarapés' in the Rio Cajari region, in Amapá State, we found this fish with a very striking coloration, which immediately caught our attention."

Although the fish looked different from known species, its appearance alone was not enough to establish that it was new to science. The team carefully examined its body proportions, counted its scales, and studied features of its skeleton. They compared these characteristics with those of closely related species and analyzed its mitochondrial DNA to determine whether it represented a distinct species.

"It was an unexpected moment," Abrantes recalled. "Initially, what most caught our attention was the impressive coloration of the males and females, which was unlike anything we had previously encountered in the study area. This sparked our admiration and a great deal of curiosity."

Genetic testing ultimately confirmed that the fish was a previously unrecognized species. For the researchers, the finding was particularly meaningful because it highlighted how much remains to be discovered in parts of the Amazon that are both poorly studied and increasingly threatened.

Once the genetic analysis confirmed the fish's distinct identity, he said, "it was something special, as we saw an opportunity to contribute to increasing our knowledge of Amazonian biodiversity and to draw attention to the conservation of areas that are still poorly explored but highly threatened."

Why Scientists Named the New Fish Laranja

The name Laimosemion laranja reflects both the fish's remarkable appearance and the place where it was discovered. In Portuguese, laranja means orange, referring to both the color and the fruit. The name also pays tribute to Laranjal do Jari, the municipality in Amapá where the species was found.

"We wanted to choose a name that would highlight a characteristic of the fish while also fostering a sense of connection with the people of the region where it was discovered," Abrantes explained.

Beyond its colorful appearance, the discovery could help scientists better understand the evolution of Amazonian killifish. Some members of this group have developed an extraordinary way to survive in habitats that periodically dry out. Their embryos can stop developing and remain dormant in damp mud, resuming development when seasonal rains refill the pools.

"Laimosemion represents one of the five independent origins of the annual life cycle within the family Rivulidae," said Abrantes. "Laimosemion laranja is particularly interesting because it expands our knowledge of the diversity and evolution of this group in the region."

Newly Discovered Amazon Fish May Already Be Endangered

Despite the excitement surrounding the discovery, the future of Laimosemion laranja is uncertain. Scientists have found it in only three small forest pools near Laranjal do Jari, and every known location shows signs of environmental disturbance.

Deforestation, mining, and urban development are putting pressure on the surrounding habitats. One of the pools is close to water that has been discolored by sediment from mining activities. Another is located within the city itself, where plastic pollution is affecting the environment.

The species' entire known range is estimated to cover just 25 square kilometers. Because its habitat is so restricted and faces multiple threats, the researchers believe the fish meets the criteria for classification as Endangered under guidelines established by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

To improve its chances of survival, the team has recommended expanding the boundaries of the nearby Rio Cajari Extractive Reserve to include the areas where the fish lives.

The discovery adds another species to the Amazon's remarkable biological diversity while underscoring the need to protect habitats that scientists have barely begun to explore. Without stronger conservation measures, species such as Laimosemion laranja could face serious threats before researchers have the opportunity to fully understand them.

The study was published in the open access journal Zoosystematics and Evolution.

Adding authenticity, Exotic was shot during a recent edition of the Exo Stars Camp, a pole-dancing camp in a Polish beach town, and includes real participants and instructors. The film will have its world premiere in the First Feature Competition of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) on Saturday, Nov. 14.

The filmmaker attended the camp herself and felt there was a story to tell. “I was fascinated by the clash of the fragile, intimate universes we carried within us around the camp,” she says. “It soon became clear that the camp itself was a perfect place to confront fears, leave one’s comfort zone and express oneself more than daily life ever allows.”

Exotic reflects that journey. It follows Mila, who is 30 and insecure. When her friend cancels on her, she reluctantly travels to a pole-dancing camp on the Polish coast alone, where she finds herself surrounded by confident dancers, skimpy costumes, high heels and a world that feels alien. But away from everyday life at home, her initial irony and unease give way to a journey of self-discovery.

Or as the PÖFF website teases: “Through demanding training, wild nights, awkward encounters, laughter, and intimate conversations, she discovers freedom, friendship, and a new relationship with herself.”

Mozaika Films is the main production company behind Exotic. The producers are Magdalena Sztorc and Anna Zajaczkowska. The cast is led by Jasmina Polak. The cinematographer was Adam Suzin, with editing handled by Tomasz Kajetan Naruszewicz. Pluto Film is handling sales.

Orlewicz-Zakrzewska talked to THR about mixing real-life experiences with fiction, how she made sure that her protagonist’s journey felt so believable and why pole dancing deserves a much better rep.

In case you don’t believe that real life inspired Exotic, just listen to the filmmaker. “I’m a pole dancer. I’ve been pole dancing for four years now,” she tells THR. “The main character in the film is played by Jasmina Polak. She’s actually a very good friend of mine in private life, and we went to pole-dancing classes together. After one or two months, we found out about the camp and decided to go together. But it was Jasmina who canceled at the last moment.”

So, Orlewicz-Zakrzewska attended the camp on her own. “Not everything in a film, but a lot of things you see are actually very much like my own experience and story,” she shares. “I did actually have those two roommates you see in the film, who were both kind of crazy in a different way. So, a lot of things there are inspired by reality.”

Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says she “fell in love with pole dancing right away.” And yes, she is aware that there still is a stigma attached to it. “There is a lot of it, and that’s why the pole-dancing community, all my girls, are really amazed by the fact that we shot this film,” she tells THR. “I did research about that and actually found out that it’s actually the first film that shows pole dance as a sport. There is no other full-length feature that shows the pole-dancing community as a sports community, as a hobby community rather than in a context of strip clubs.”

What does she love about it? “There are so many things,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says. “First, it’s an amazing workout. Your core strength is insane. For me, the gym is so boring. I also really like the femininity in this dance. And the more strength you have, the more effortless and, in a sense, more feminine and graceful you look. And then in your mind, the strength links up with the feminine.”

Exotic also shows the fun and party aspects that can come with the workouts. “I really love the fact that it has this entourage” and community spirit, explains Orlewicz-Zakrzewska. “The reason why I never explored it [before she started pole dancing] was that I was scared of judgment. I was scared of the patriarchal eye. There is a certain judgmental eye towards the pole-dancing community.”

How about the skimpy outfits? “You do often wear almost nothing, which actually makes a lot of sense because of the sweat and because you need your skin to hold on,” the filmmaker explains. “And the high-heeled shoes actually make a lot of sense when doing the spins [or jumps].”

And wearing these outfits and pole dancing opened her up to accepting a side of her that she was not willing to even consider before. “I have never been a girly girl,” shares Orlewicz-Zakrzewska. “I have always been a little bit intellectual and ran around with boys and climbed trees and so on. But I always had this other side in me, and [pole-dancing allowed me to] explore this more open form of femininity.”

Showcasing pole dancing and its community is something that excited the filmmaker and the folks at the camp. The writer-director actually knew right away that she would return to the post-Soviet hotel, where the camp takes place, with the camera. And she did.

But how did she approach the shoot and getting the people at the camp involved? “Before it started, I told the participants [and instructors] that I wanted to shoot the film. Is everybody okay with that? If anybody’s not, just please say no,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska recalls saying. “And imagine: nobody said no. Not a single person! Because they are performers, and most people in pole dancing are really open. So, they were really happy that we were doing this film and showing this community the way it really is.”

So keep your eyes open for non-professional actors in Exotic! “All is scripted, but we were just putting our actresses and actors inside the actual situations, inside the actual classes,” the director explains.

Exotic also features a 2007 clip of Jonas Mekas, the late Lithuanian filmmaker and poet who has been called “the godfather of American avant-garde cinema,” defending Paris Hilton. He argued that society has become too negative and skeptical to believe that people can actually change.

Which gets us to the question of Mila’s change in Exotic. Her transformation is neither instantaneous nor dramatic, and that is by design. The filmmaker recalls her experience at Exo Stars Campo. “It’s just really, really intense, you are outside of your everyday social bubble and you really have to confront the question of how you want to be perceived by others,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska tells THR. “It’s about both your relationship with yourself and also your relationship with the people you meet. So there are mechanisms that help you grow internally and reflect. But at the same time, nothing really happens because it’s just a sports camp. There are limitations to the massiveness of the internal journey.”

Her conclusion: “It’s not that a real revolution is going to happen there. But there is maybe the seed of the revolution that you are going to carry on with you.”

Exotic is Orlewicz-Zakrzewska’s first feature film, but it wasn’t supposed to be. “I was actually working on two other big projects before, but this one happened to get finished first,” she tells THR, adding with a laugh. “Maybe the reason why Exotic was produced as the first one is that it’s the most ‘normal’ thing I ever wrote. All the other things are much crazier.”

So, what’s next for her? “I’m working on two other feature films and a series,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska says. “But all of these things are in development.”

It will be interesting to see if her next project has a short title, just like Exotic, or a really long one. After all, the title of her debut feature went through an evolution. “What’s funny is that with the titles for the things I write, it’s always either a full, super-long sentence or just one word. It’s never in between,” Orlewicz-Zakrzewska explains. And she shares the first title she had for Exotic, and it is indeed long: If the World Is Round, I Don’t Know What It Means to Be Ahead.

#709. Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared. The extraordinarily rare discovery is giving researchers a new understanding of how some of Earth's earliest marine animals lived, fed, and evolved.

The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish. Crinoids often resemble underwater flowers, with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these unusual creatures were among the animals thriving in Earth's earliest coral reefs, long before plants and animals had become widespread on land.

Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures. Delicate body parts usually decay long before fossilization can occur, leaving major gaps in our understanding of how these ancient creatures functioned.

Now, paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare specimen that preserves soft tissue structures, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate life in Earth's ancient oceans.

"After an animal dies, soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are the first things to decay," said Dr. Lena Cole, OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. "Most fossils are only made up of hard parts like bones, teeth, or shells. Soft tissues are only preserved when the environment acts almost like a natural refrigerator or vacuum‑sealer -- conditions that are incredibly rare."

A 450 Million-Year-Old Fossil With Exceptionally Rare Soft Tissue

The remarkable specimen belongs to Dendrocrinus simcoensis, an extinct species of crinoid. Its preserved tube feet represent only the second known example of fossilized soft tissue in crinoids and the oldest such discovery ever documented.

Tube feet are small, flexible structures found in echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and crinoids. Because these structures are soft and easily destroyed after death, finding evidence of them in fossils is extraordinarily unusual.

"Preservation like this is truly one in a million," Cole added. "Crinoid fossils number in the millions, and this is only the second time soft tissues have ever been found."

The age of the specimen makes the discovery even more remarkable. These delicate structures have been preserved in the fossil record for nearly half a billion years, offering direct evidence of anatomy that would otherwise have disappeared.

"It's incredible these soft tissues have survived more than 450 million years," said Dr. David Wright, another OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, who co‑authored the study with Cole. "For reference, these soft tissues are more than 200 million years older than the oldest dinosaur."

Ancient Feeding Structures Reveal Evolutionary Secrets

The fossil's preserved tube feet are especially valuable because they provide clues about how crinoids obtained food and interacted with their surroundings.

Unlike the teeth and jaws that many familiar animals use to eat, crinoids rely on specialized structures to capture food particles from seawater. Their tube feet play an important role in feeding and in how these animals interact with ocean currents.

The size, arrangement, and shape of these structures can differ between species, reflecting adaptations to particular habitats and feeding methods. By studying those differences, paleontologists can reconstruct aspects of an extinct animal's lifestyle, even when no living examples of that species exist.

"Since crinoid tube feet are used for feeding, you can think of them in a similar way to how we think about teeth in mammals," Wright explained. "Differences in their structure tell us about what kinds of environments a species lived in and how it fed."

Researchers also compared the ancient fossil with crinoids living in today's oceans. Those comparisons revealed notable anatomical differences, suggesting that the feeding structures of these animals have undergone substantial evolutionary changes over hundreds of millions of years.

"Comparisons with living crinoids show that the anatomy of this ancient species was very different," Cole added. "This gives us new insight into how crinoids evolved and how their feeding strategies changed over hundreds of millions of years."

A Rare Window Into Earth's Earliest Ocean Ecosystems

Beyond revealing details about one ancient species, the discovery could help scientists piece together how marine ecosystems developed during the early Paleozoic Era.

The Paleozoic was a vast chapter of Earth's history that began about 541 million years ago. During its early stages, marine environments supported an expanding variety of complex animals, while life on land was still relatively limited.

Crinoids were among the creatures that became established in early reef communities. Their fossils provide important evidence of how marine animals occupied different ecological roles and adapted to changing environmental conditions.

However, studying only living species cannot reveal the full range of forms and adaptations that existed in the distant past. Some extinct animals possessed anatomical features that have no close equivalent among their modern relatives.

"Fossilized remains of long‑extinct species can show features well outside the range of variation we see in living species," Wright said.

"By comparing ecological ways of life for extinct and modern species, we can understand how patterns of adaptive evolution have changed through time and what factors shaped the modern biosphere."

The biosphere includes all living organisms on Earth and the environments they inhabit. Understanding how it developed requires scientists to examine not only which species existed, but also how they interacted with their surroundings and one another.

Because soft tissues are so rarely preserved in ancient echinoderms, discoveries like this one provide evidence that conventional fossils cannot offer. They can help researchers identify previously unknown feeding strategies, understand ancient ecosystems, and trace evolutionary changes that eventually shaped modern marine life.

An Extraordinary Discovery Hidden in a Museum Collection

Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is where the fossil was found.

Although major paleontological breakthroughs are often associated with expeditions to remote locations, valuable scientific evidence can also remain unnoticed for decades in museums.

Fossil collections contain enormous numbers of specimens, many of which have never been examined by specialists with the expertise needed to recognize their most important features. As scientific knowledge and research methods improve, these collections can reveal discoveries that earlier generations overlooked.

"New fossil discoveries ultimately come from fieldwork, but museum collections play a significant role in this kind of integrative research," Wright said. "We don't always know the full significance of the specimens we collect. New technologies, ideas or expertise often find surprising ways to utilize existing specimens to make new discoveries."

The Dendrocrinus simcoensis fossil had been housed for years at Montréal's Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution, a small museum that operates entirely with support from community donations.

Its remarkable scientific value became apparent when Cole and Wright, both specialists in crinoids, visited the museum and examined the specimen more closely.

Their investigation revealed that the fossil preserved an extraordinarily rare record of ancient soft tissue, transforming a specimen already held in a museum collection into an important source of new evolutionary evidence.

"This discovery highlights the importance of museum collections and the community support that keeps them alive," Cole said. "Without the dedication of many people caring for these collections, this research would never have been possible."

More Discoveries May Be Waiting in Museum Drawers

The finding also demonstrates why preserving and maintaining fossil collections is essential for future research.

At the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Cole and Wright oversee invertebrate paleontology collections containing more than one million specimens. Additional fossils are added every year, creating new opportunities to investigate ancient organisms and identify previously unrecognized species.

With collections of this size, no individual researcher could possibly examine every specimen in detail. A fossil that appears ordinary today might become the focus of a major discovery when studied by someone with a different specialty or new scientific tools.

Making collections available to researchers around the world increases the chances that these overlooked treasures will eventually receive the attention they deserve.

"This is why we work to make our collections accessible to researchers around the world," Wright said. "There are simply too many fossils to study over one person's career. There's more than a lifetime's worth of discoveries waiting to be found."

The extraordinary crinoid fossil is a reminder that some of the most revealing clues about Earth's distant past may already have been collected. They are simply waiting for someone to recognize what makes them special.

Materials provided by University of Oklahoma. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"No NASA mission has ever done this before."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Twin NASA spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long escapade, ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet.

The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) spacecraft launched in November 2025 on the second-ever flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. But rather than head straight to Mars, the two spacecraft dawdled through a looping trajectory. Now, they are back in Earth's neighborhood where they tackled a crucial engine burn unusually close to Earth that — if all goes well — will set them on track for Mars.

"No NASA mission has ever done this before," said Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and principal investigator of the ESCAPADE mission. "For most missions, it just isn't necessary."

That's because traditionally NASA's Mars missions have been carefully choreographed within cosmic launch constraints, leaving Earth during a brief window of planetary alignment that only occurs every 26 months. ESCAPADE was meant to launch in October 2024, when Earth and Mars were favorably aligned, but delays with the New Glenn rocket forced the mission to sit out the precious launch window.

Rather than wait to launch this fall, NASA decided to try something new. ESCAPADE mission planners designed a "loitering" orbit, shaped like a kidney bean. It called for the twin probes to loop through that trajectory to be back at Earth in early November 2026, ready to continue on to Mars.

Once they arrived, however, the twin probes faced a major hurdle: Each had to perfectly execute an engine burn within Earth's gravity well. The maneuver is similar to the slingshot flybys that spacecraft regularly conduct to adjust their trajectories — but here, the probes had to fire their engines to amp up the effect of the burn rather than acting alone.

The first spacecraft tackled the feat on Nov. 7; the second did so on Monday (Nov. 9). And according to NASA, the burns went perfectly. "This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we've now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days," Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for NASA's Heliophysics Division said in a statement.

After just a few minor course corrections, ESCAPADE will be sailing toward a September 2027 Mars arrival.

The twin ESCAPADE spacecraft have made the most of their extended tour. Each spacecraft is about the size of two refrigerators and equipped with three scientific instruments and a couple cameras. All are tailored for studying the strange magnetic field of Mars, which is created both globally by charged particles from the sun interacting with the atmosphere and locally by areas of highly magnetic crust.

Earth's magnetic field is much stronger and generated by the planet's core. But it too is affected by the solar wind, as scientists call the constant stream of charged particles flowing off the sun and across space. On the side of Earth opposite the sun, the solar wind stretches the magnetic field to form an elongated tail structure, like a terrestrial windsock.

A range of missions have studied this magnetotail at various points up to nearly 800,000 miles (1.27 million kilometers) away from Earth, but beyond that, it has been a mystery. Conveniently, the two ESCAPADE spacecraft traveled through the structure over the course of about 10 days early last year at a much greater distance from Earth — some 1.19 million miles (1.91 million km) away.

"We were able to capture the magnetic field structure of that distant tail, how it flaps, how it moves, how the plasma flows within it," Lillis said, gathering data that he called "unprecedented." "And not only that but for the first time, we were able to do that with two spacecraft simultaneously."

A second shot at the magnetotail came over the summer, when the spacecraft were much closer to Earth but the moon was also passing through the magnetic structure. The two ESCAPADE spacecraft were able to partner with twin ARTEMIS-THEMIS spacecraft at the moon to observe the structure from four different perspectives simultaneously.

That's a huge boon when trying to study the magnetotail and its intricate and ever-changing magnetic field lines and plasma, Lillis said. "These are generally not things you can measure remotely," he said. "You kind of have to be there."

Meghan Bartels is a freelance science journalist based in New York City who worked on staff for Space.com from 2018 to 2023. Her writing has also appeared in outlets including Scientific American, Science News, Wired, Newsweek and Audubon.
